text: He checked his bank account, and saw a hundred and twenty thousand dollars that wasn't his.
The day before, he had just eleven hundred dollars.
One teller made one mistake. The money was meant for a business.
So he asked himself one question. Is it mine now?
He didn't call the bank. He went shopping.
Fifteen thousand dollars down on an SUV.
Two four-wheelers. A camper. A race car.
Then fifteen thousand more, handed out to friends.
In two and a half weeks, over a hundred thousand dollars was gone.
Then the bank noticed.
It pulled the money back out. All of it.
His balance dropped to minus a hundred and seven thousand dollars.
The bank called. His wife picked up.
She said they'd work out a way to pay it back.
Then they stopped answering.
So who's right? The bank made the mistake.
Can a bank really make you pay for its own error?
Then the police knocked on the door.
Police say they admitted the money wasn't theirs.
The charges? Theft, and receiving stolen property.
Here's the answer. A bank's mistake is still the bank's money.
If you know it's not yours and spend it, that can be theft.
This really happened to a couple in Pennsylvania, in 2019.
Would you have called the bank, or gone shopping? Comment one.
